- Where the valves are declared, as evidence for owner decision (3). A temporary Tomcat 9.0.121 with a WAR that holds `META-INF/context.xml` with a `SemaphoreValve` applied it: with `concurrency="${probe.concurrency}"` and the system property 2, two of four concurrent requests were answered and two got 503. The attribute `${probe.undefined:-7}` with no property gave 7 answers and 2 refusals of 9, so a default in the file works. A host descriptor `conf/Catalina/localhost/probe.xml` with concurrency 1 replaced the valve of the WAR (one answer, three refusals), it did not add to it. The launcher writes a `Host` with `appBase="webapps"`, `unpackWARs="true"` and `autoDeploy="false"` and copies each WAR to `webapps/<name>.war`; the test fixture does the same with `autoDeploy="true"`; the installation page puts each WAR in the `webapps/` of its instance; none sets `deployXML`, whose default is true. The pom already gives each WAR its own `web.xml` under `src/main/org/epics/archiverappliance/<component>/WEB-INF` and adds files through `webResources`, so a `META-INF/context.xml` per component fits the same pattern. In a declaration in `server.xml` or in the `conf/context.xml` of an instance, an operator edits one file per instance; in the WAR no operator step is needed.
- How the tests get low thresholds: the system properties of the extra JVM options that step 3 adds, with a default in the `context.xml` of the WAR, or a host descriptor in the `conf/Catalina/localhost` of the test base; no file is generated for the first.
- PVAccess calls at a time: the library runs an RPC call inline on the receive thread of the TCP connection that carried it (the thread name was `TCP receiver`). A call of 2 s took 2,008 ms alone, two calls on one connection took 4,003 ms (they queue), two calls on two connections took 2,002 ms. The `PVAServer.POOL` (the common pool, 15 threads here, 1 at `-XX:ActiveProcessorCount=2`) serves search replies only. The server therefore bounds nothing: the concurrency is the number of connections, and a long call holds the others of its connection.
- What an HTTP client receives, as evidence for owner decision (2), from a servlet on Tomcat 9.0.121. Before the commit, `sendError(400)` gave a 400 and an exception gave a 500, with a page. After the commit: letting the exception go ended the connection and the client read `Premature EOF` after status 200, which any HTTP client can tell from a complete answer; `sendError` was refused (`IllegalStateException`) and the body ended normally; swallowing the exception, which `DataRetrievalServlet` does today, gave a complete 200; an error record at the end of the body gave a complete 200 that holds the record. Only the first is told from a complete answer by every client and in every format; a record needs a place in each of the nine formats (`json`, `csv`, `txt`, `svg`, `mat`, `qw`, `flx`, `jplot`, `raw`), which the mime responses of `retrieval/mimeresponses` do not have. What the application itself sends is read, not executed here; T3 and T7 run it.
- What a PVAccess client receives: no answer until its own timeout (the executions recorded with owner decision (4)).
- Findings outside the loops of this row, entered as rows M86 and M87 in the Backlog by D53: the PVAccess answer that is copied at every event and held whole, also for a raw read; the PVAccess server that bounds neither the calls at a time nor their duration, so the valves do not reach it.

Step 3, the fixture (2026-10-21, JDK 21.0.12.1, Tomcat 9.0.121). `TomcatSetup` takes, before a setUp method: `withJvmOptions(...)` for the CATALINA_OPTS of every child Tomcat (a heap such as `-Xmx256m`, the options of the first layer, and the system properties that the valve attributes of decision (3) read as `${name:-default}`); `withEngineBackgroundProcessorDelay(seconds)` for the Engine of the generated `server.xml`; `withJmx()` for a free loopback port of JMX on each child, with `jmxPort(appliance)` and `currentThreadsBusy(appliance)` reading the `ThreadPool` bean of the connector (the Tomcat of the fixture runs the four web applications in one JVM, so the value is the sum over them). It keeps the child by appliance name, with `exitStatus(appliance)`, `waitForExit(appliance, timeout, unit)` and `consoleLines(appliance)`. The reader of the console now goes on to the end of the stream; before, it stopped when the process was no longer alive and lost the last lines. `Process.destroy()` closes that pipe at once, so the last lines of a child are read only when it ends by itself or by a signal that leaves the pipe open (`toHandle().destroy()`), as an OutOfMemoryError exit does. The valve attributes of the plan reach the child through the system properties, not through the generated `server.xml`.
- Checked: `TomcatSetupOptionsTest` (new, 2 tests: the child JVM holds the heap option, the property option and the tag, the Engine reports the delay of 1 s, `currentThreadsBusy` is read over JMX, the console holds the start-up line; the exit status and the lines after the end are read), 2 passed in 75 s; `TomcatSetupTest` 2 passed; `RetrievalOperatorRequestTest` 6 and `MultiPVClusterRetrievalTest` 3 passed, which start the fixture singly and as a cluster.

The sampler recorded every one of the 91 child lifetimes identified by the fixture's startup log. Each sampler started 0 to 1 ms after its matching startup record and became ready before test requests; its records include child PID, sample count, first/last and start/end timestamps, monotonic elapsed time, maximum sample gap and capture outcome. The concurrent console workload requests each of 15 pages and its static dependencies in three rounds, including CSS references and JavaScript module imports; it does not execute browser scripts or their BPL calls. These measurements read the shared connector across all four applications, not separate context maxima, and a sampled maximum is not a guaranteed instantaneous peak. T6 class verification, 2026-10-22. `RetrievalMemoryProtection` selects the actual old-generation pool, reads collection usage, rate-limits explicit collection, counts allocation since the request began and checks interruption independently of memory pressure and the allocation floor. Its explicit `Settings` have no deployment defaults. `CallableEventStream` guards input before post-processing while preserving `RemotableOverRaw`; both HTTP and PVAccess consumers check output events. Tests exercised the real input wrapper and both output loops, declared point-count rejection including 2^31-1, the allocation floor above and below pressure, admission recovery after releasing live objects without a separate allocating workload, and the startup WARN in a child JVM with DisableExplicitGC. Fallback was exercised with the real allocation counter disabled and through a live standard ThreadMXBean JMX proxy exposing no allocation extension; the pressure fallback used the existing estimate. These are class/stream checks, not HTTP or PVAccess network acceptance.

Step 6 endpoint preparation, 2026-10-22 02:33 PDT. RetrievalState owns one explicitly configured protection instance shared by HTTP and PVA. DataRetrievalServlet scopes GET/POST retrieval, PvaGetPVData scopes each action, and each GetDataAtTime store worker starts and closes its own scope on its executing thread. Declared admission runs before estimateMemoryConsumption and any point-array allocation; estimates remain available for the allocation-counter fallback. The request budget accumulates across postprocessors. CAPlotBinning declarations and the allocation loops that fill missing optimized bins and construct plot output also participate in the checks. Pipeline failures are unwrapped from futures and propagated; failed consumers omit normal finalization. An uncommitted HTTP response is reset and receives 400 for declared size, 503 for a protection rejection or 500 for another processing failure; a committed response throws IOException to the container. PVA throws PvaActionException with the cause and message.

RetrievalProtectedRequestTest passed seven cases using the shipped GenerateData, ConfigServiceForTests, PlainPB store, servlet, PVA action and postprocessors. The checks cover both point-count operators at 2^31-1 in all nine HTTP formats, multi-PV admission, combined budgets through HTTP GET/POST and the multi-PV PVA action, output interruption before/after HTTP commit, the per-appliance worker path returning the requested stored timestamps, PVA refusal and subsequent normal requests. Only the HTTP request/response transport boundary is substituted. These checks establish servlet/action behavior, not Tomcat connection truncation or a PVA client's timeout. The initial raw-request input and missing fixture appliance/store metadata were corrected; their unsuccessful outputs remain in work/m85-step6-requests-01.log and work/m85-step6-requests-03.log.

The observer recorded 1,782 samples. In 35 samples, collection usage was below the 174,483,046-byte pressure threshold while current old-generation usage was above it. One sample read collection usage 171,946,104 bytes (163.98 MiB), current old-generation usage 179,127,176 bytes (170.83 MiB) and total heap usage 244,102,552 bytes (232.79 MiB); the three separate reads spanned 2,964 ns. Thus the collectedUsage method before the correction could receive a below-threshold collection value after current old-generation usage had exceeded the threshold. At that time, the method used the collection value both to trigger explicit GC and to decide rejection. The observation establishes delayed input to the check, not the direct cause of the historical OOM. Sampling is not atomic and adds 655,360 bytes of fixed arrays plus headers and counter-read allocation; this observed run is diagnostic evidence, not a headroom bound or production-setting qualification. Protected valve observations, 2026-10-22 10:41 to 10:49 PDT. protected-valves-mat-03 passed two tests with no failures/errors/skips in 94.204 s on unchanged source/WAR/store inputs. At 4 GiB with candidate memory settings and deliberate concurrency 2, stuck/interrupt thresholds 1 s and Engine background delay 1 s, three excess retrieval requests returned valve 503 in 7 ms. The two admitted optimized_1000000 MAT requests stopped at the production protection check and returned 503 with Retrieval request interrupted in 1402 and 1403 ms. No declared-budget, memory-admission or pressure rejection bypassed the interrupt check, and a normal query recovered on the same JVM. The management overload check returned three valve 503 responses in 6 ms and completed two actual five-second searches, followed by recovery. The fixture now observes 250 ms of zero busy connector threads before the management workload; the earlier run observed four refusals and remains a failed exposure under protected-valves-01.

The earlier committed-response interruption check failed before the deadline correction. A real 30-day raw CSV response was already status 200 with a body byte received when the external reader paused. Tomcat recorded a valve interrupt at 1467 ms, but the client subsequently received the complete 94,935,387-byte response with normal EOF at 2107 ms. protected-valves-jfr-02 reproduced complete EOF at 2134 ms. Its jdk.JavaExceptionThrow record places InterruptedException on the same request thread in Object.wait and NioEndpoint$NioSocketWrapper.doWrite at line 1898. The installed Tomcat 9.0.121 bytecode catches that exception and resumes its write loop without restoring the interrupt. The existing protection check reads the current interrupt flag, so this path loses the cancellation signal. This is an observed product failure, not missing pressure or a successful truncation.

The earlier JSON overload assertion also expected precommit 503 even though those responses had already committed. JFR records both RetrievalMemoryProtection$Rejected from Request.check and the servlet's Retrieval response interrupted exception, as well as a separate Tomcat NioChannel interrupt exception; the original native failures remain retained. MAT provides the actual precommit case above. No claim is made that a chunk-format error alone proves a protection check.

PVA connection diagnosis, 2026-10-22 12:48 to 12:51 PDT. pva-disconnect-512m-01 repeated the real 20,001-bin single control with client JUL FINE capture and the unchanged 30-second EPICS_PVA_CONN_TMO. ClientTCPHandler.checkResponsiveness logged `idle for 32886ms, closing` at 19:49:53.518473465Z; the loaded channel entered INIT at 19:49:53.518724519Z and reconnected at 19:49:59.164069939Z. The client sent repeated ECHO requests before closure. The retained server stack at elapsed 33.016 seconds was still inside PvaMimeResponse.appendStructureArray, PVAStructureArray.set and cloneType on the TCP receiver. The actual core-pva 5.0.5 bytecode calls the RPC service synchronously on that receiver and handles ECHO messages through the same receive loop. Its client checks responsiveness every three seconds at this setting and closes after more than 30 seconds without a life sign. This execution identifies the client responsiveness check as the shutdown initiator while response construction prevents the server receiver from handling the queued connection checks.

The server finished constructing the answer after 56,539 ms total, including 56,518 ms in consolidated output, then logged SocketException: Socket is closed. The original client future reached its unchanged 120-second wait limit. Native outcome: one test error, zero assertion failures/skips, exit 1, 171.289 seconds including fixture startup/teardown. The pair, third-request admission and recovery assertions were not reached. All 1,606 JMX samples belong to the single control; maximum collection usage was 158,009,552 bytes, below admission 268,435,456 bytes, and sampled maximum heap usage was 469,558,792 bytes. No memory-pressure rejection or OOM was observed. Diagnosis is established; admission remains Incomplete and T8 remains Partial. Reproducing this timeout is not a passing protection test or a performance comparison.

The 600,001 and 700,001-bin results expose a test judgment limitation: it observes collection usage before sending the probe, while the production admission check can perform a collection and accept normally. The current test treats that valid response as an immediate assertion failure and ends observation of the fitting pair. The correction subsequently accepted by option 1 is to record a normal probe response and continue observing within the unchanged pair deadline, then require the actual client/server memory refusal value to be between the heap's admission and pressure bounds, both original responses to complete identically, quiescence and same-channel recovery. Actual pressure remains a failure and missing refusal remains Incomplete; no thresholds, timeout extension, external GC or internal substitute is proposed. The buffer-setting decision alone did not authorize this change; the subsequent option 1 decision recorded above accepts and authorizes it. Verification is required before any updated pass claim.

#### M86 - Build the PVAccess answer without copying its array at every event

Origin: daff1b7 / M86
Identity History: none
GitHub Issue: none
Status: Complete

##### Summary

PVAccess retrieval retains each complete answer until transmission. PvaMimeResponse accumulates the samples of the current PV in an ArrayList, checks each incoming sample against that PV's element type, and creates its PVAStructureArray at the next PV boundary or response close. Label and variant arrays are created at response close. Names, supported types, event order, values and empty-PV representation are preserved; repeated whole-array copying and repeated validation of all earlier samples are removed.

##### Scope

- The arrays of the PVAccess answer are built without a copy per event, for example from a list that is turned into the array once when the PV or the stream is closed.
- A test over several event counts compares the allocation of the thread, which grows by a factor of about four when the events double on the old code and about two on the new.
- The answer, as a client reads it, is the same: `PvaGetPVDataTest` and the other PVAccess integration classes pass.

Out of scope: the size of the answer (M85 bounds a request by memory); the shape of the PVAccess answer; the PVAccess calls at a time (M87).

##### Completion Criteria

- The allocation of a PVAccess answer grows linearly with its events: doubling the events about doubles the allocation.
- The answer is the same as before for every case of the existing PVAccess tests.
- The default suite and the PVAccess integration classes pass.

##### Dependencies And Decisions

- D53 (Decision Date 2026-10-21): entered from the audit of M85.
- D54 (Decision Date 2026-10-22): assigned before the next M85 / T8 workload selection; this is the chosen work order, not proof that every possible T8 input depends on M86.

##### Implementation Plan

Plan Status: accepted
Plan Acceptance: 2026-10-22; option 1 selects M86 response-construction improvement before resuming T8 input selection.
Implementation Authorization: 2026-10-22; option 1 authorizes the existing allocation and response-equivalence plan.
Superseded Plan Artifacts: none

1. Measure the allocation of `PvaMimeResponse` over 5,000, 10,000 and 20,000 events. Check: T1.
2. Replace the three appends by collections finalized at PV boundaries and response close, preserving names, types, event order and values. Check: T1 and T2.
3. Run the default suite and the existing PVA integration classes on rebuilt WARs; retain the original failure and compare real old/new response contents. Check: T2.

#### M83 - Delete the moved partition of a zip store that is an ETL source

Origin: daff1b7 / M83
Identity History: none
GitHub Issue: #52 (https://github.com/jeonghanlee/epicsarchiverap-maven/issues/52)
Status: Not started

##### Summary

A `pb` store with `compress=ZIP_PER_PV` that is the source of an ETL move keeps the partition it moved: `getETLStreams` keys each `ETLInfo` with `path.toAbsolutePath().toString()`, which for a path inside the zip file system is the entry's path without the `jar:` prefix; `markForDeletion` resolves that key on the local file system, finds nothing and ignores the `NoSuchFileException` by design, so the entry stays and the samples exist twice. `getETLStreamsForDeletion` keys its rows in the `jar:` form, so the explicit deletion works. Observed on 2026-10-19 with the shipped `ETLJob` over STS HOUR to a zip MTS HOUR with `pp=mean_60` to LTS YEAR: the LTS held the data and the archive still held both `.pb` and both `.mean_60` entries. A zip store is meant as the last store of a chain, where no move starts, so the shipped configurations do not reach this (D47).

##### Scope

- `getETLStreams` keys the `ETLInfo` of a zip path in the `jar:` form through the same helper as `getETLStreamsForDeletion`, so `markForDeletion` deletes the moved entry and its post-processor entries.
- A test over two hops with a zip MTS, which keeps the moved partition today, passes.

Out of scope: the uncompressed store (M80); where a zip store may sit in a chain (the book says the last store).

##### Completion Criteria

- After a move out of a zip store the archive no longer holds the `.pb` entry of the moved partition nor its post-processor entries, and the next store holds the data once.
- The explicit deletion of a PV from a zip store keeps working.
- The default suite passes.

##### Dependencies And Decisions

- D47 (Decision Date 2026-10-19): left to the Backlog for a later release; found by the check of M80.

##### Implementation Plan

Plan Status: draft
Plan Acceptance: none
Implementation Authorization: none
Superseded Plan Artifacts: none

1. The key of `getETLStreams` through the shared helper. Check: T1.
2. The two-hop case with a zip MTS added to `PlainPBPostProcessorCleanupTest`. Check: T1.

#### M87 - Bound the concurrent calls of the PVAccess retrieval service

Origin: daff1b7 / M87
Identity History: none
GitHub Issue: none
Status: Not started

##### Summary

The PVAccess server of `core-pva` 5.0.5 runs an RPC call on the receive thread of the TCP connection that carried it (executed on 2026-10-21 in the audit of M85: a call of 2 s took 2,008 ms alone, two calls on one connection took 4,003 ms, two calls on two connections took 2,002 ms). It sets no limit on the connections and none on the calls at a time, and a long call holds the other calls of its connection. The Tomcat valves of M85 do not reach it, because the PVAccess server is not behind the Tomcat pipeline. M85 bounds a request by the memory it declares and the memory pressure, but the number of PVAccess retrievals in flight, each holding its answer whole (M86), is not bounded.

##### Scope

- The retrieval PVAccess service (`PvaDataRetrievalService`) takes a permit for each call and refuses the call when none is free, with a message in the log of the retrieval application; as for any refused PVAccess call, the caller sees its own timeout (decision (4) of M85).
- The number of permits is a measured value; the valve concurrency that M85 chooses is its starting point.

Out of scope: the duration of a call, which no layer bounds in PVAccess; the management PVAccess service (`PvaMgmtService`); the HTTP valves (M85).

##### Completion Criteria

- With more long calls than permits, on separate connections, the permits are used and the next call is refused with a message in the log of the retrieval application.
- When a call ends, the next call is accepted.
- The default suite and the PVAccess integration classes pass.

##### Dependencies And Decisions

- D53 (Decision Date 2026-10-21): entered from the audit of M85; it does not block M85 or the merge.
- Open at the plan: the number of permits; whether the duration of a call is bounded and how; whether the management service takes the same limiter.

##### Implementation Plan

Plan Status: draft
Plan Acceptance: none
Implementation Authorization: none
Superseded Plan Artifacts: none

1. A limiter class with a fixed number of permits that never waits. Check: T1.
2. The retrieval service takes a permit around each call and releases it in a `finally`. Check: T1 and T2.

##### Test Plan

| Label | Layer | Method | Environment | Expected Result |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| T1 | Unit | The limiter with more concurrent takers than permits, and a release | JDK 21 | Only the permits are granted, the others are refused at once, and a released permit is granted again |
| T2 | Integration | A PVAccess retrieval service with a call that takes long, called from more connections than permits, with the logger of the library on | JDK 21, Tomcat 9.0.121, `softIocPVX` | The calls up to the permits are answered, the next is refused with a message in the log, a call after one has ended is answered; fails on the old code |

#### M88 - Verify signal storage and important-signal delivery under client overload

Origin: daff1b7 / M88
Identity History: none
GitHub Issue: #55 - https://github.com/jeonghanlee/epicsarchiverap-maven/issues/55
Status: Deferred

##### Summary

Verify appliance behavior under excessive client requests according to the operational priorities: first, signal storage; second, storage and delivery of important signals; last, client request handling. Rejecting or stopping client requests is acceptable when required to preserve the higher-priority functions. Process survival and memory thresholds alone do not establish this behavior.

##### Scope

- Combine real IOC updates, actual archiving and delivery, and concurrent HTTP/PVA retrieval load in an isolated appliance using the intended deployment layout.
- Compare emitted sequence numbers, values and timestamps with stored records and destination receipts before, during and after overload; account explicitly for configured sampling and deadband.
- Cover oversized requests, concurrent accumulation, in-flight memory growth, slow or disconnected clients, repeated retries and repeated overload/recovery cycles.
- Retain memory, GC, worker and connection observations to explain the storage, delivery, rejection and recovery results. Keep controlled-exposure checks separate from operation without test-driven GC or filesystem read holds.

Out of scope: immediate implementation or execution; changing M85 / T6, T7 or T8 completion criteria; selecting a new collector, admission policy or signal-priority mechanism without a separate accepted plan.

##### Completion Criteria

- An accepted contract defines important signals, delivery destinations and protocols, expected stored/delivered records, allowed delays and client rejection/recovery behavior.
- Real combined-load tests demonstrate the required storage and important-signal delivery throughout overload, with no unexplained missing, duplicated or corrupted records against that contract.
- Excessive requests are refused or stopped with observable failure, and request handling recovers within the agreed bound without restarting the appliance; failures and missing exposure remain explicit.

##### Dependencies And Decisions

- Decision Date: 2026-10-22. Retain this work as a long-term Backlog plan; exclude it from current execution. Existing M85 scope and completion criteria remain unchanged.
- Priority order: signal storage; important-signal storage and delivery; client requests.
- Related evidence: M85 request-protection measurements and M87 concurrency planning. No execution dependency is assigned by this record.
- Open planning details: important-signal selection, delivery semantics, allowable storage/delivery latency, client behavior during overload, deployment resources and observation duration. These are future plan inputs, not permission to implement.

##### Implementation Plan

Plan Status: draft
Plan Acceptance: none
Implementation Authorization: none
Superseded Plan Artifacts: none

1. Define the operational contract and record a normal-load baseline with independently observed IOC emissions, stored records and delivery receipts. Check: T1.
2. Combine continuous signal production with the overload scenarios and normal client probes, judging storage and important-signal delivery before request service. Check: T2.
3. Repeat overload/recovery cycles and the selected heap profiles; verify final data integrity and resource recovery. Check: T3.

##### Test Plan

| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| T1 | Operational baseline | Observe real IOC emissions, stored records, important-signal delivery receipts and normal client responses | Isolated appliance; resources and signal contract to be defined | Actual records and delays satisfy the accepted contract before overload |
| T2 | Combined-load integration | Continue T1 production while applying oversized, concurrent, growing, slow/disconnected and retrying HTTP/PVA requests | Same appliance and signal contract; no substituted internal request path | Storage and important-signal delivery meet their higher-priority requirements; client requests complete correctly or fail observably |
| T3 | Repeated recovery | Repeat normal/overload/recovery cycles and selected heap profiles; compare final records and worker/connection state | Same deployed code; duration and limits to be defined | Data integrity and agreed recovery bounds hold without restart or accumulating abandoned work |
